title: Taiwan’s Janet Chen Brings Breaststroke Power to Fresno State—and She’s Just Getting Started
summary: For Janet Chen, the pool has always been a place of quiet determination. Now, that determination is taking her over 6,000 miles from home. The Taiwanese swimmer, a World Junior Championships qualifier, has officially committed to Fresno State University, where she’ll hit the water as a Bulldog in the fall of 2026. “I’m incredibly grateful for the endless support from my family and coaches,” Chen said. “I’m honored to continue my academic and swimming career at Fresno State.” Chen, who hails from Hsinchu City and trains with the Taiwanese Swimming Federation, is primarily a breaststroke and freestyle specialist. Her international debut came at the 2025 World Aquatics Junior Championships (long course meters), where she placed 27th in the 50 breast (32.88), 33rd in the 100 breast (1:15.39), 51st in the 50 free (27.25), and 60th in the 100 free (1:00.15). She also led off Taiwan’s 800 free relay with a lifetime best 2:18.28. Since then, Chen has been systematically demolishing her own records. At the 2025 Yunlin National Games, she clocked a personal-best 26.67 in the 50 free. Weeks later at the 3rd Asian Youth Games, she dropped her 50 breast to 32.37. Most recently, at the 2026 National High School Games, she posted a 1:13.28 in the 100 breast and a 4:38.24 in the 400 IM—both lifetime bests. Based on converted times from the 2026 Mountain West Conference Championships, Chen would have landed in the ‘C’ final of the 50 free and 100 breast, giving her a real shot at scoring early for the Bulldogs. She’s projected to rank among the team’s top three in those events, though incoming freshmen could shuffle the deck. Chen will be joined by Aliz Szilvási-Hazag (free/fly/IM), Bella Benes and Aylah Angeles (diving), and Emma Price (free/IM)—a promising cohort that could lift Fresno State in the coming years. For a swimmer who’s been quietly stacking personal bests, the move to Division I is a bold next chapter. And if her trajectory holds, Janet Chen is just getting warmed up.
why_it_matters: Janet Chen's story shows how international student-athletes use sports as a pathway to higher education and broader competition, highlighting the global nature of college recruiting and the importance of steady improvement in turning far‑away dreams into reality.

background_read: College athletics in the United States, especially NCAA Division I (the top level of U.S. college sports), draws student-athletes from around the world, offering both education and high-level competition.

Swimming programs often recruit internationally, converting times between long course meters (used in most international meets) and short course yards (used in U.S. college pools) to gauge performance.
Fresno State, a Division I university in California’s Central Valley, competes in the Mountain West Conference and has a history of developing swimmers from different countries.
The Taiwanese Swimming Federation is the national governing body for competitive swimming in Taiwan, overseeing training and athlete development like Janet Chen's.

Janet Chen’s personal bests in breaststroke and freestyle have been steadily dropping, a sign of focused training and a rising trajectory that mirrors a growing trend of Taiwanese athletes seeking opportunities in the American collegiate system.

perspectives.description: Chen’s rapid improvement and commitment to a Division I program show that disciplined training can open doors to education and top‑tier competition. Her progress could inspire other young swimmers in Taiwan and around the world.
Some may worry about the pressures of adapting to a new country, academic rigor, and the demanding schedule of NCAA swimming, which has led to burnout for many international recruits.

From a numbers standpoint, her converted times place her as a solid mid‑level conference scorer, indicating that while she’s talented, she will need further development to become a dominant force in the NCAA.

If Chen continues her trend of personal bests, she could move into scoring range at the conference level and perhaps qualify for higher‑level meets like the NCAA Championships. Her journey may also encourage more Taiwanese swimmers to pursue U.S. collegiate programs, strengthening a global talent pipeline.
